## 1. Identify the top 3 suburbs with the highest number of property transactions over the years, and plot their monthly transaction counts for the year 2022. Include Toorak in the plot as well, if it is not among the top 3 suburbs.

### Data cleaning

Check how many row contains NA cases.

```{R}
ptv %>% 
  filter(
    if_any(everything(), is.na)
  )
```

Since a all 418390 rows contains NA fields, we will clean them as we work through each section based on the context of task requirements.

(SHOULD WE CONSIDER ONLY VICTORIA ?????)

```{R}
ptv %>% count(state) 
```

Observe cases with NA state.

```{R}
ptv %>% filter(
  is.na(state)
)
```

We observe all 21 cases with NA state are empty meaning less cases. We will simply drop of these cases later.

Observe cases with NA suburb.

```{R}
ptv %>% filter(is.na(suburb))
```

We observe all 21 cases with NA suburb are empty meaningless cases, which are the same as before.

Observe badge to check if we can filter by sold records.

```{R}
ptv %>% count(badge)
```

We observe all 21 cases with NA badge are empty meaningless cases, which are the same as before. The remaining are labelled "Sold".

Observe any NA date or out of range date (we are only interested in 2010-2023).

```{R}
ptv %>% 
  filter(
    is.na(ymd(sold_date)) |
    year(sold_date) < 2010 |
    year(sold_date) > 2023  
  ) %>%
  select(id, sold_date) %>%
  arrange(sold_date)
```

We observe 5218 cases contain NA sold date.

Observe if other fields hints us on how to impute the NA sold_date.

```{R}
ptv %>% 
  filter(
    is.na(ymd(sold_date))
  )
```

Since no other fields allow us to impute sold date, we will drop off all cases with NA sold date.

```{R}
ptv_cleaned <- ptv %>%
  filter(
    # remove the 21 meaningless NA rows
    !if_all(everything(), is.na),
    # Vic only
    state == "Vic",
    # remove NA sold_date
    !is.na(ymd(sold_date))
  )

ptv_cleaned
```

### Obtaining top 3 suburb with highest total transaction across the year (2010-2023)

Group ptv_cleaned by suburb and get the total transaction of each suburb over the years (2010-2023)

```{R}
ptv_cleaned %>%
  group_by(
    suburb
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    total_transaction_suburb = n()
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_transaction_suburb))
```

The top 3 suburb with highest number of property transaction over the years are:

1.  Toorak

2.  Melbourne

3.  Clyde North

We will save the 3 suburb names into a top_3_suburb table.

```{R}
top_3_suburb <- ptv_cleaned %>%
  group_by(
    suburb
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    total_transaction_suburb = n()
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_transaction_suburb)) %>%
  select(suburb) %>%
  head(3)

top_3_suburb
```

### Obtain month transaction count in year 2022 of the top 3 suburbs

To get the monthly transaction counts for year 2022 of these 3 suburb, we semi-join the top_3_suburb table with ptv_cleaned by suburb field. Then extract the year and month from sold_date field. Filter only rows from year 2022 and calculate the sum of transaction per month by grouping suburb and month.

```{R}
# monthly transaction counts for the year 2022

top_3_monthly_transaction_2022 <- ptv_cleaned %>%
  semi_join(
    top_3_suburb,
    by = "suburb"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(sold_date),
    month = month(sold_date)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    year == 2022
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    suburb,
    month
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    total_transaction = n()
  )
  

top_3_monthly_transaction_2022
```

We observe:

1.  Clyde North has 12 months.
2.  Melbourne has 12 months.
3.  Toorak has only 11 months. (WHAT TO DOOOOO)

### Monthly Transaction Count of 2022 by Suburb Visualisation

We use a line chart to plot monthly transaction counts for the year 2022, with each suburb differentiated by the line color. A line chart is used because transaction count over time is continuous data, where the slope of the line viisualises trends, patterns and rate of change throughout 2022. Colored lines allows direct comparison of month-to-month trajectories across the 3 suburbs on a single plot.

```{R}
ggplot(top_3_monthly_transaction_2022, aes(x = month, y = total_transaction, color = suburb)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 1:12,            
    labels = month.abb
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Transaction Count of 2022 by Suburb",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Total Transaction",
    color = "Suburb"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 2. What are the 3 most important keywords in the description column that impact property prices? (Note: Since the description column contains a large volume of text, please extract a 10% sample from the original dataset to answer this question.)

### Data cleaning

Since the description column contains a large volume of text, we will extract 10% sample from the original dataset for this analysis.

Observe price.

```{R}
ptv_cleaned %>% count(price) %>% arrange(desc(price))
```

We observe price has inconsistent categorisation, for example:

1.  Range: \$XXXXXX- \$YYYYYY; that overlaps
2.  Contact agent
3.  \$ZZZZZZ

To standardize the price, we will convert all price to numeric value instead of range-base because:

1.  Range-based field disregards information such as the difference between \$980,000 - \$1,140,000.
2.  Goal is to measure how keywords relate to price, which works best with a continuous price.

We will create a new price_num column where the original price will be parse as such:

1.  Raw value with "Contact agent" will result in NA after parsing, which will then be dropped off since there is no price signal.

2.  Raw value of "\$ZZZ,ZZZ" is parsed to numerical ZZZZZZ

3.  Raw value of "Range: \$XXXXXX- \$YYYYYY" is parse to obtain the midpoint value.

Observe description.

```{R}
ptv_cleaned %>% head(10) %>% select(description)
```

We observe description fields are textual data.

Observe any NA description.

```{R}
empty_desc <- ptv_cleaned %>% filter(is.na(description))
```

We will drop cases with NA description since no informational keywords-price relationship can be obtained if the description is NA itself.

Compiling all the observation from price and description column, we create the new ptv_price table.

```{R}
# helper function to parse range-based price into numerical price
parse_price <- function(x) {
  # extract numerical value from string (eg: $XXX,XXX into XXXXXX)
  nums <- str_extract_all(x, "[0-9]{1,3}(,[0-9]{3})+|[0-9]{5,}")
  
  # get the midpoint from range-based price
  map_dbl(nums, ~ if (length(.x) == 0) NA_real_
                else mean(as.numeric(str_remove_all(.x, ",")))) 
}

ptv_price <- ptv_cleaned %>%
  mutate(
    # parse price into numerical
    price_num = parse_price(price)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    # exclude NA description
    !is.na(description),
    # exclude invalid negative price 
    price_num > 0,
    # exclude NA price_num 
    # (eg: price that are originally have no price signal like "Contact agent")
    !is.na(price_num)
  )

ptv_price %>% select(id, price_num, price, description) %>% arrange(desc(price_num))
```

Extract the 10% from ptv_price table.

```{R}
# use seed for reproducibility
set.seed(5145)

ptv_10_perc_sample <- ptv_price %>% slice_sample(prop = 0.10)

ptv_10_perc_sample %>% select(id, price_num, price, description) %>% arrange(desc(price_num))
```

### Pre-processing textual data

```{R}
desc <- ptv_10_perc_sample %>%
  mutate(
    doc_id = row_number()
  ) %>%
  select(
    doc_id,
    text = description
  )

desc <- as.data.frame(desc)

desc_source <- DataframeSource(desc)
desc_corpus <- Corpus(desc_source)

desc_corpus
```

Observe the first row in desc_corpus.

```{R}
inspect(desc_corpus[1:1])
```

Text removal using:

1.  Case normalization to lowercase: Ensures stop words can be matched consistently regardless of capitalization.
2.  Remove stop words: Eliminate common words that don't carry much meaning.
3.  Remove punctuation: Remove punctuation that don't contribute to the meaning of text.
4.  Remove numbers: Numerical digits do not contribute much to the meaning of text
5.  Strip whitespace: For consistency.

```{R}
desc_corpus <- tm_map(desc_corpus, content_transformer(tolower))

desc_corpus <- tm_map(desc_corpus, removeWords, stopwords("english")) 

desc_corpus <- tm_map(desc_corpus, removePunctuation)

desc_corpus <- tm_map(desc_corpus, removeNumbers)

desc_corpus <- tm_map(desc_corpus, stripWhitespace)

```

Observe the first row in desc_corpus after text removal.

```{R}
inspect(desc_corpus[1:1])
```

We will reduce words to their base forms to reduce sparsity and improve the efficiency and accuracy of text analysis in description column. Lemmatisation technique is used because we want the output to be a valid word (unlike stemming technique that may return partial/prefixes/suffix of an original word).

```{R}
# define helper function to lemmatise text
lemmatize_text <- function(text) {
  lemmatised <- lemmatize_strings(text)
  return (lemmatised)
}

desc_lemma <- tm_map(desc_corpus, content_transformer(lemmatize_text))
```

Inspect the first row in desc_lemma after lemmatisation.

```{R}
inspect(desc_lemma[1])
```

Verify if all the 10% descriptions exist in desc_lemma.

```{R}
length(desc_lemma)
```

### Feature extraction

After text pre-processing, we will represent the pre-processed words as numerical expression.

We will build a Document Term Matrix called desc_dtm to observe the sparsity

```{R}
desc_dtm <- DocumentTermMatrix(desc_lemma)

inspect(desc_dtm)
```

We observed:

- Sparsity = 100%, indicating 100% of values in matrix is zero. However, this is due to rounding up as calculated from (3110421323 - 3712687)/3110421323 \* 100% = 99.88%.

Remove sparse term from desc_dtm. Sparse value (= x) used means if term appears less than (x \* 100%) in all documents, we remove it. We try 3 different sparse values: 0.99, 0.98, 0.95

```{R}
desc_dtm_spar_099 <- removeSparseTerms(desc_dtm, 0.99)

inspect(desc_dtm_spar_099)
```

```{R}
desc_dtm_spar_098 <- removeSparseTerms(desc_dtm, 0.98)

inspect(desc_dtm_spar_098)
```

```{R}
desc_dtm_spar_095 <- removeSparseTerms(desc_dtm, 0.95)

inspect(desc_dtm_spar_095)
```

```{R}
term_freq <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(desc_dtm_spar_095) > 0) * 1

term_freq
```
